<!-- section:why -->

A setting or a compositional rule is useful only when it serves your intention. This lesson helps you explain a choice and inspect its consequence.

<!-- section:understand -->

The edge of a photograph decides what context is included and what is cut off. Inspect all four edges before capture, especially bright intrusions and awkward partial objects. Look once at the subject, then trace the perimeter deliberately. This brief second pass catches distractions that central attention can miss.

<!-- section:see -->

In a fictional café scene, the subject is clear but a bright half-visible menu intrudes from the right. Compare shifting position, changing the crop, and including the menu fully. Each changes the context; none is automatically correct.

<!-- section:deeper -->

Removing all background detail can erase useful context. Keep an element when it supports place, scale, or the intended story.

<!-- section:customer -->

This wider frame keeps the café context, while the tighter version emphasizes expression. The choice follows the story we want to tell.

<!-- section:try -->

A travel portrait has a clipped landmark at the top edge. Give two defensible alternatives and explain their different intentions.

<!-- section:revisit -->

Include the landmark deliberately to preserve the sense of place, or reframe tightly enough that it no longer distracts from the person. Compare both before choosing.
